ECE 6390

Parity constraints as a graph

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a parity-check matrix and its graph express allowed codewords and inconsistent observations.

A binary parity-check matrix H assigns one XOR equation to each row. For a column codewordc, the legal-word condition is Hc =0 mod 2. A graph draws bit variables as circles and check equations as squares, with an edge exactly where the corresponding H entry is 1.

The six-bit teaching graph uses checks c₁⊕c₃⊕c₄ =0, c₂⊕c₃⊕c₅ =0 and c₁⊕c₂⊕c₃⊕c₆ =0. These checks match the earlier block code. The syndrome H r records failed checks for a received columnr. A zero syndrome establishes membership in this code, not that the transmitted information was necessarily recovered.

LDPC means low-density parity-check. Practical long-block LDPC codes have a sparse H and iterative decoders that exchange soft messages among connected variables and checks. Sparsity refers to H; the generator matrix need not be sparse. The tiny graph explains this notation and does not represent a real DVB-S2 block or error-performance prediction.

The adjustable figure flips up to two positions of the teaching word and highlights its syndrome. The full codebook permits an independent nearest-Hamming comparison. Several bit patterns can share a syndrome; correcting beyond the code’s stated distance guarantee can select a wrong legal word. BCH and LDPC are distinct stages in the DVB-S2 protection chain.

Example

For legal word 101010, all three checks are 0. Flipping its sixth bit gives 101011 and syndrome 001: only the third check fails. In this distance-three teaching code, the syndrome identifies that single flipped position, but a different multi-bit pattern can produce the same syndrome.

Practice

1. Why can a zero syndrome fail to prove that no channel error occurred?

Compare the received word with every possible legal transmitted word.

An error can change one valid codeword into another. The received word then satisfies every parity constraint while representing different information.

2. Must a generator matrix G be sparse for a code to be called LDPC?

The family’s name identifies its sparse matrix.

The defining sparsity is in the parity-check matrix H. A valid generator can be much denser; it serves a different mapping role.
